### Introduction to Jude — Authorship
- Green: letter names author “Jude” (Ἰούδας) per Greco-Roman/Semitic letter convention; self-identifies as “a slave of Jesus Christ and brother of James.” | "naming the author “Jude”… “a slave of Jesus Christ and brother of James”" | L993 [jude] [jude-brother-of-jesus] [james-the-just]
- Green (via Ilan): Ἰούδας transliterates יְהוּדָה; 179 Palestinian occurrences; very common patriarchal/tribal name; never a gentile name → author Jewish. | "179 occurrences of the name יְהוּדָה… “Jude” never appears as the name of a gentile" | L993
- Green eliminates other NT Judases: not Iscariot, Galilean revolutionary, Damascus host, Barsabbas; not the apostle “son of James” (Luke 6:16 etc.) because author is *brother* not son of James. | "this apostle could not be the author of the book since he was a son of someone called James and not his brother" | L995
- Green’s identification: “Jude… brother of James” = sibling of Jesus listed in Matt 13:55 / Mark 6:3; likely youngest or next-to-youngest male. | "most likely the same person who is named, along with James, as one of the siblings of Jesus (Matt. 13:55; Mark 6:3)" | L997 [jude-brother-of-jesus]
- Green: “brothers of the Lord” known widely, engaged in missionary activity (1 Cor 9:5); sometimes with Mary (suggesting Joseph’s earlier death). | "The “brothers of the Lord” were known widely… appear to have engaged in missionary activity (1 Cor. 9:5)" | L997
- Green: James without qualification = “Lord’s brother,” Jerusalem “pillar” (Gal 2:9), resurrection witness (1 Cor 15:7), leader after Peter’s departure (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18); Jude claims shared familial honor/authority paralleling (but not identical to) Paul’s apostolic claims. | "by identifying himself as the “brother of James,” Jude makes a claim to authority that parallels Paul’s affirmations of his apostleship… not identical with apostleship" | L999 [james-the-just]
- Green surveys early confusion: some call Jude “apostle”; Bede equates with Thaddeus; Syriac tradition conflates with Thomas (Gospel of Thomas opening; Eusebius Eccl. Hist. 1.13.10). Clement of Alexandria stresses Jude’s reluctance to call himself the Lord’s brother, preferring “servant… brother of James.” | "yet did not say that he himself was His brother… ‘Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ,’… but ‘the brother of James.’" | L1001–L1003
- Green: bishop lists (Epiphanius; Apostolic Constitutions) place Jude among early Jerusalem bishops after James/Simeon; Eusebius differs (Justus as third); cannot ground epistle authorship in these lists. | "we cannot draw from it any conclusions regarding the authorship of the epistle. The internal evidence from the NT, however, favors identifying Jude as the brother of Jesus and James" | L1005–L1009
- Green (via Bauckham) on Jesus’s siblings: Helvidian (Joseph+Mary), Epiphanian (Joseph’s prior marriage), Hieronymian (cousins). Green: most accessible reading = half-brothers (Helvidian); Epiphanian possible but less probable and “distinctly theological” to preserve Mary’s perpetual virginity. | "the most accessible reading would be that they were children of this union, and as such half brothers of Jesus… “to preserve the honour of Mary”… distinctly theological" | L1011 [jude-brother-of-jesus]
- Green on ancient canonicity doubts: accepted widely in West and Alexandria; Syrian churches slow; Peshitta excluded Jude (with 2 Pet, 2–3 John, Rev); included in Philoxenus 507/508. Eusebius classed Jude among “disputed” books publicly read; Origen notes doubts yet treats as Holy Scripture. | "Jude was one of the “disputed” books… What doubts did arise about the authenticity of Jude can be traced primarily to the epistle’s use of 1 Enoch" | L1015–L1017 [jude] [jude-1-enoch-canon]
- Green: Jerome accepts Jude despite Enoch quotation (“rejected by many… by age and use it has gained authority”); Tertullian uses Jude to authenticate 1 Enoch; Augustine accepts Jude as canonical while rejecting Enoch as genuine. | "because in it he quotes from the apocryphal book of Enoch it is rejected by many… Enoch possesses a testimony in the Apostle Jude… while Jude is canonical, Enoch should not be accepted" | L1017 [1-enoch]
- Green: early positive reception includes Muratorian Canon and Athanasius; Clement wrote a commentary for gentile audience on a letter with “strong flavors of Palestinian Judaism.” Proposed second-century allusions (Bigg/Chaine lists) are “vague”/“scanty and shadowy”—not compelling for authenticity. | "parallels produced are not compelling… At best we could say that Jude fits neatly into the conceptual and linguistic frame of the fathers" | L1019–L1021
- Green: strongest early use-testimony is 2 Peter ch. 2’s extensive reproduction of Jude (Peter used Jude); weight varies with 2 Peter’s authorship/date, but even early-second-century 2 Peter still evidences Jude’s early date/use. | "the second chapter of 2 Peter reproduces much of Jude… only if we suppose that Peter used Jude" | L1023 [2-peter-jude-relationship] [2-peter-authorship]
- Modern objections Green engages: (1) refined Greek style / Hellenization vs Galilean literacy (Oleson, Kelly, J. Charles; Horsley on elite literacy); (2) “post-apostolic” tone of vv. 17–18; (3) second-century gnostic opponents.
- Green’s style response: brothers engaged itinerant ministry → Greek fluency; secretaries common (Rom 16:22; 1 Pet 5:12; papyri pen-changes); scribes could take dictation or larger literary role—“Jude should not be rejected on stylistic grounds.” | "most likely made use of the services of a secretary… Jude should not be rejected on stylistic grounds" | L1029–L1031 [gene-green]

Green/Koester Antioch): Green rejects—Jude excluded from Syrian canon until Philoxenus; Thomas-Jude conflation doesn’t prove origin. | "falls hard on the historical evidence that the epistle was excluded from the Syrian canon until the sixth-century edition of Philoxenus" | L1045–L1047

- Green prefers first-century Palestinian Christianity (Bauckham, Gerdmar, J. Charles): unqualified “James” (v. 1) best where James known; relatives of Jesus linked to Palestine (exc. 1 Cor 9:5); Hegesippus/Eusebius on Domitian and Jude’s peasant grandsons with church leadership; family land in Nazareth/Kokhaba; midrashic/Qumran-pesher-style exegesis; Assumption of Moses best known in Palestinian Jewish Christian circles. | "third suggestion is that the epistle finds its roots within the world of Palestinian Christianity of the first century. The weight of the historical evidence in favor of this reading is impressive" | L1057–L1059
- Greek-language problem for Palestinian audience: Green posits sizable Hellenistic Jewish (Diaspora-raised) and gentile populations in Palestine (Caesarea, Sepphoris, Decapolis, etc.); God-fearers not necessarily strong in moral/theological embrace of Torah; libertinism not unthinkable among Jews (Sir 9:2–9; agape proximity temptations). | "converts to whom Jude writes likely included a considerable number of gentiles who lived in Palestine… The kind of temptations the recipients of Jude faced were not foreign to Palestine" | L1061–L1069
- Green on desposynoi / family circle: Jesus’s family exercised leadership parallel to apostolate (1 Cor 9:5); James leader of Jerusalem; descendants of Jude held property and leadership; not “dynastic” royalty—self-designation as slaves of Christ; Domitian scene shows economic humility (9,000 denarii / 39 plethra, hard hands). | "We should not, however, think of James, Jude, and the others as holding dynastic leadership… no large estate or inheritance" | L1071–L1073 [jude-brother-of-jesus] [james-the-just]
- Synthesis of provenance: early Palestinian Christianity opening to gentile mission; shared sphere with James and (via misused grace teaching) Paul; 2 Peter’s use of Jude also signals Palestinian Christian sphere. | "brings us into contact with early Palestinian Christianity that was in the process of opening up to the gentile mission" | L1075 [2-peter-jude-relationship]
- Date factors listed by Green: authenticity; heresy century; Pauline-misreading link; 2 Peter literary order; “postapostolic” reading of v. 17; early-catholic tradition (v. 3). Parallels 1 Cor (~54/55) and Romans (~55–58). **Latter part of 50s or first half of 60s.** | "sometime in the latter part of the 50s or the first half of the 60s of the first century" | L1081–L1083 [jude]

### Opponents
- Occasion: Jude intended a letter on “common salvation” (v. 3) but was constrained to write because ungodly teachers infiltrated from outside, perverting grace into license and thus denying “the only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.” | "Jude did not write the letter he originally intended… teachers whose conduct was ungodly and whose doctrine was a perversion of the teaching on grace had come in from the outside (v. 4)" | L1087 [jude]
- Dual pastoral aim: contend for once-for-all faith (v. 3); build up/stand firm (vv. 20–21); mercy for waverers (v. 22); rescue those fallen (“Snatch some from the fire,” v. 23) without rescuers being ensnared—primary focus “gospel and the community.” | "Jude’s primary focus, therefore, is on the gospel and the community" | L1089
- Profile Green draws: new spin on grace as freedom from moral constraint (v. 4); knew Christian teaching, perhaps Pauline; present at agape (v. 12); denial of Lord is practical not defective Christology (contrast 2 Peter on former genuine discipleship); reject authority (v. 8a) and “glories”/angels (v. 8b)—possibly because Jewish theology saw angels as law-mediators (Acts 7:53; Gal 3:19); claim divine dreams over against apostolic tradition. | "the denial of which Jude speaks is practical… New, inspired revelation was set over against apostolic tradition" | L1093 [2-peter-jude-relationship] [michael-archangel]
- Broad label “antinomianism”: sexual license; avarice; blasphemy/slander/grumbling/arrogance/mockery; shameless lack of self-control; ungodly; not Spirit-led but animal instincts; soulish not spiritual (v. 19); itinerant teachers infiltrating by stealth; flatterers “shepherding themselves”; cause divisions. Presence = last-times sign (v. 18); God can keep disciples (v. 24). | "Not a few authors have broadly characterized the error as “antinomianism.”… Their presence, in effect, is a sign that the last times have arrived" | L1095–L1097
- Rhetoric: “these are” vs “but you” draws sharp boundary (vituperatio / rhetoric of slander); formative for church, not persuasion of heretics; uses commonplaces of vice but with case-specific application (agape seduction; flattery in persuasion; slander of glories). Green (vs du Toit): stereotyping does not erase historical particularity when names/specifics attached (Quintilian). | "Jude employs these conventional charges in ways specific to the situation his readers faced" | L1099–L1107
- Same opponents as 2 Peter? Common assumption from literary dependence; Green rejects automatic identity (analogy: Synoptics share sources, not audiences). Fornberg: Jude stresses sexual immorality; 2 Peter defective eschatology (3:1–10). Neyrey/Bauckham: 2 Peter’s opponents under Epicurean-style denial of providence/prophecy—not in Jude. Shared antinomianism, but Jude’s opponents claim dream-inspiration (Jude 8) unlike 2 Peter’s. Peter skillfully reused Jude against different libertines. | "both the foundations and the results of the error are distinct in these two cases" | L1109–L1111 [2-peter-jude-relationship]
- Gnostic/Carpocratian identification: Sidebottom/Kelly “incipient gnosticism”; Carpocrates (Alexandria, early second century)—angel-creators, magic, dream-demons, radical license, common wives after agape (Clement Strom. 3.2); Clement quotes Jude “prophetically.” Green: similarities striking but differences decisive—Carpocratians separatist with own feasts vs Jude’s infiltrators in apostolic-tradition church; Clement treats Jude as earlier prophetic text, not contemporaneous; no matter/spirit dualism polemic; no world-creating-angels cosmology required by “slander glories”; antinomianism from misread grace not equality/common property; no extreme Carpocratian orgy/magic/equality-with-Jesus features. “Highly unlikely that Jude addresses this or any other gnostic sect.” If authentic first-century Jude, cannot combat Carpocratians. | "It is highly unlikely that Jude addresses this or any other gnostic sect… the epistle could not have been written to combat the Carpocratians or any other gnostics" | L1113–L1121 [jude]
- Green’s non-precise ID within mid-first-century fabric: inspired novelty vs received faith; covetous, arrogant, anti-authority; grace allows unrestrained sexuality; no place for law. Church must fight, be built up, rescue—no negotiation; finality of sacred tradition at stake. | "Jude makes no attempt to negotiate and find a common ground… The finality of the faith that was handed down as sacred tradition was at stake" | L1125–L1127

### Use of 1 Enoch / Assumption of Moses / canon
- Green: extrabiblical material woven in—angelic fall (v. 6) from Gen 6:1–4 elaborated in 1 En. 6–12; Michael vs devil over Moses’s body (v. 9) from Assumption/Testament of Moses; explicit quotation of 1 En. 1.9 (vv. 14–15). | "That Jude knows, echoes, and even quotes this literature is beyond dispute" | L1131 [jude-1-enoch-canon] [1-enoch] [michael-archangel]
- **Option 1 — Canonize sources because Jude used them:** Tertullian (Apparel of Women 1.3) and Clement of Alexandria; Noah could preserve/renew Enoch; “Enoch possesses a testimony in the apostle Jude”; Clement: Jude “confirms the Assumption of Moses” and “verifies the prophecy.” | "if these books were good enough for Jude, then they were good enough for them" | L1133–L1135 [1-enoch]
- Reception of 1 Enoch pre-Jude: not Hebrew-canon, but dynamic use (Nickelsburg)—Jubilees invests Watchers material with authority; 11 MSS at Qumran Cave 4 + Book of Giants; Sirach, Wisdom, 4 Ezra, etc. Assumption/Testament of Moses early first century AD (Tromp); Jude assumes reader familiarity. | "Jude’s esteem of 1 Enoch was not out of harmony with the honor ascribed to the book by some circles within Judaism" | L1137–L1139
- Green notes broader NT/early-church Enoch use: basis for 1 Pet 3:18–22 (Dalton); Barnabas cites as “Scripture”; Papias, Apoc. Pet., Gospel of Peter, Justin, Athenagoras, Irenaeus know Watchers; contemporary authority mainly Ethiopian Church and LDS. Late date undermines Tertullian’s Noah-preservation claim. | "in the contemporary church, this book is not considered to be authoritative except by the Ethiopian Church and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints" | L1141–L1143 [1-enoch] [enoch]
- **Option 2 — Question Jude for using pseudepigrapha:** rabbinic severity on Gen 6:1–4 Enochic reading; Didymus and Jerome note many rejected Jude for this; Apostolic Constitutions brands Enoch “pernicious.” Modern church keeps Jude’s canonicity but practically marginalizes the book (Rowston “most neglected”). | "practical marginalization of Jude since it is viewed as a problem more than a source of faith" | L1145–L1147 [jude-1-enoch-canon]
- **Option 3 (dominant) — Accept Jude, not his sources:** possible early witness if 2 Peter omits Jude’s explicit apocryphal uses; Augustine City of God 15.23 / 18.38—some truth in apocrypha but no canonical authority; Enoch wrote by inspiration per Jude, yet books not genuine / excluded from temple canon. Green: Augustine affirms truth of quoted parts but “did not fully answer the question.” | "we will accept Jude but not count the sources from which he drew as authoritative" | L1149–L1155
- Popular “authentic fragment” theory (1 En. 1.9 truly from historic Enoch): Green calls it often “special pleading”; fails for Assumption of Moses v. 9; pre-Noah survival remote; circular if defended only from Jude. | "appears as nothing more than special pleading… neither this nor Augustine’s view account for Jude’s appeal to the Assumption… of Moses in verse 9" | L1157
- “All truth is God’s truth” / Paul-quotes-pagans analogy (Chaine, M. Green, J. Charles, Moo): Green rejects—Jude’s intro formula equals OT prophecy presentation; Enoch = “seventh from Adam”; only Enoch and apostles get recorded words as authorities for “marked out for this judgment” (v. 4); places 1 Enoch with Torah (vv. 5–6, 11), Moses-burial tradition (v. 9), and apostles (vv. 17–18). “Jude evokes 1 Enoch as predictive and authoritative revelation.” | "Jude’s use of 1 Enoch… is different from Paul’s occasional appeal to Greek authors. Jude evokes 1 Enoch as predictive and authoritative revelation" | L1159–L1161 [jude-1-enoch-canon]
- Green’s constructive line: Jude judicious—eschews fanciful material; focuses canonical themes (transgression of order vv. 6, 9; judgment of unrighteous vv. 14–15); each incident tied to set canonical texts (Gen 6; Deut 34:5–6 + Zech 3:1–2; Deut 33:2 via 1 En. 1.9). “closer to canonical bedrock than is sometimes acknowledged.” | "Jude makes judicious and limited use of references to apocryphal literature… closer to canonical bedrock than is sometimes acknowledged" | L1163–L1165
- Ad hominem “opponents’ book” theory (J. Charles et al.): Green rejects—quotation marks 1 Enoch authoritative for Jude himself; letter to church not opponents; “even” reading of καί is conjecture driven by theological protection of OT canon. Tension remains between inspiration theology and historical investigation; “Perhaps we have still not gone beyond Augustine’s marvelous wisdom.” | "J. Charles’s conclusion is more theological than historical/exegetical… We can come only to limited conclusions with the evidence we have" | L1167–L1169 [jude-1-enoch-canon]

### Genre and structure / rhetoric
- Form: Hellenistic letter opening (author, recipients, greeting vv. 1–2) + closing doxology (vv. 24–25) instead of standard Greco-Roman/Semitic closings (farewell, health wish, autograph, etc.). | "Jude opts not to follow any of the normal Hellenistic or Semitic conventions of letter closings" | L1173 [jude]
- Watson: forensic-rhetoric outline (epistolary prescript quasi-exordium 1–2; exordium 3; narratio 4; probatio 5–16; peroratio 17–23; doxology quasi-peroratio 24–25); yet classifies Jude as deliberative relying on epideictic; “middle style.” Neyrey: true forensic. | "deliberative rhetoric which relies heavily upon epideictic… Neyrey… forensic rhetoric" | L1183–L1207
- J. Charles: “word of exhortation” / synagogue homily pattern (cf. Acts 13 logos paraklēseōs); Bauckham: “epistolary sermon”; Neyrey/Perkins stress letter with rhetorical body conventions.
- Green’s counter: oral reading of letters does not convert them into oratory; ancient theory distinguishes letter style from public discourse (Seneca, Demetrius, Aristotle, Cicero). Jude is a “letter of exhortation,” not oral word of exhortation retrofitted. Fits Pseudo-Demetrius advisory/vituperative and Pseudo-Libanius paraenetic types; “beloved” = friendship convention for paraenesis. | "Jude composed a genuine letter and not an oral discourse… a “letter of exhortation.”… we need not resort to rhetorical theory to explain its contents and structure" | L1213–L1227 [gene-green]
- Closing doxology: Christian epistolary development (Rom 16:25–27; 2 Pet 3:18; 1 Clem., etc.), not proof of sermon; functions like Greco-Roman closings to rehearse letter themes (Weima)—assurance God keeps them blameless vs heretics (v. 4). | "While the form of Jude’s closing is different… its function is the same" | L1229–L1233
- Body structure (Ellis/Bauckham midrash): series of authoritative texts (OT, Pseudepigrapha, apostolic prophecy) + “these/these are” comments (vv. 8, 10, 12, 16, 19); midrash as contemporizing exegesis, not later rabbinic forms; affinities and differences with Qumran pesharim; typology + direct fulfillment (Enoch + apostolic prophecy). Brackets with “remember” (vv. 5, 17). | "the body of the letter is primarily structured around a series of authoritative “texts” and their application… heretics were entities known by God, who had predicted beforehand both their coming and their doom" | L1235–L1241

### Theology / purpose
- Green’s integrated purpose claim: contend for once-delivered faith against grace-turned-to-license; pastoral rescue of waverers/fallen; confidence in God’s keeping power (doxology); apocalyptic framing of opponents as last-days markers; non-Pauline Palestinian Christian voice in dialogue with misused Pauline grace teaching. | "This letter exhorts the believers facing the error to be built up and stand firm in the faith… Yet Jude’s confidence in this situation rests in God (vv. 24–25)" | L1089–L1097; L1127 [jude] [theosis-divine-nature]
- No freestanding “Theology of Jude” section in this range; theological claims are embedded in authorship, occasion, opponents, pseudepigrapha, and structure discussions (as Green’s preface promised: theology woven with history). | "theological concerns of the letters are woven together with the contextual and historical discussions" | L177

#### Green’s outline of Jude (for integrator reference)
- I. Epistolary greeting (1–2): author Jude; recipients the called; wish-prayer mercy/peace/love
- II. Letter body (3–23): purpose disclosure (3–4); call to remember—texts/fulfillment (5–19: Exodus/angels/Sodom; Michael/devil; Cain/Balaam/Korah; Enoch prophecy; apostolic prophecy + “these are” comments); exhortations (20–23)
- III. Closing doxology (24–25)
